questions.prompt: In a hypothetical (if-then) proposition, the antecedent is:
choices: A The part after “then.”
B The part between “if” and “then.”
C Always a disjunction.
D The Latin name for an invalid mood.
questions.explain: If–antecedent–then–consequent. Those labels also name the mixed argument forms.

questions.prompt: Affirming the antecedent (modus ponens) is the pattern:
choices: A If P then Q; P; therefore Q — and it is valid.
B If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q — and it is valid.
C If P then Q; Q; therefore P — and it is valid.
D Either P or Q; P; therefore not Q always.
questions.explain: Second premise affirms the if-clause; you may draw the then-clause. Valid; later named modus ponens.

questions.prompt: Denying the antecedent is invalid because, in the Roberto example:
choices: A Working hard is the only possible cause of tiredness.
B Not working hard does not rule out other ways of becoming tired.
C If-then sentences cannot be symbolized.
D It is identical to modus tollens.
questions.explain: Hard work is one route to tiredness; gym, sleeplessness, etc. can still make him tired.

questions.prompt: Denying the consequent (modus tollens) is illustrated by:
choices: A If fire then oxygen; no oxygen; therefore no fire.
B If fire then oxygen; oxygen; therefore fire.
C If fire then oxygen; no fire; therefore no oxygen.
D Either fire or oxygen; fire; therefore oxygen.
questions.explain: If fire then oxygen; there is no oxygen; so there is no fire. Valid; called denying the consequent / modus tollens.

questions.prompt: Which mixed hypothetical forms receive Latin names here, and why does Hicks joke about the others?
choices: A Only the invalid ones get Latin names because they are elite mistakes.
B Affirming the antecedent (modus ponens) and denying the consequent (modus tollens); the invalid pair are “so bad they don’t deserve a Latin name.”
C All six forms are called Barbara.
D Disjunctive syllogisms are all named modus ponens.
questions.explain: The two valid mixed forms get MP / MT; denying the antecedent and affirming the consequent do not get Latin honorifics.
